Mr. Speaker, I am confident that if hon. members would refer to the Canada Gazette of January 2, they would be somewhat bewildered by the ambiguous tariffs under which the Canadian Performing Right Society operates. I am not at all concerned about the tariffs and fees they collect from theatres or broadcasting stations, because those institutions are well able to look after themselves. But the continuous complaints from small music users in the interior of British Columbia, from such places as lodge halls, orchestras, skating rinks, stores and the like, together with the unjust fees the society seeks to collect, certainly suggests that there should be some remedy for the existing situation.
The society in coming into a community attempts to collect a minimum of $30. If it cannot get the S30, it will come back next day and indicate its willingness to take S20. If it cannot get S20, it will take $10. The purpose seems to be to get money some way. It is not a satisfactory way, because most of its collections are induced by threats. At the last session of parliament we had an extended review of the set-up of the Canadian Performing Right Society. Hon. members will recall that there was an American Society of Authors, Composers and Publishers, and an English society with which were affiliated various associations in the different European countries. Those societies are about fifty per cent publishers. The publishers are the people who acquire the copyrights on various pieces of music, and are those who profit chiefly by such fees as can be collected.
There are about twelve hundred members in the American societies and an equal number in the English and affiliated societies.

Copyright Amendment-Mr. Esling
The directors of the two societies apparently saw a fertile field in Canada for the collection of money, and as a result in 1925 the Canadian Performing Right Society was incorporated under the Dominion Companies Act. It had a capital set-up of 10,000 no-par-value shares. To show that there was very little Canadian interest in the matter, may I say that only seven of the 10,000 were retained in Canada as qualifying shares.
Prior to the time of Judge Parker's investigation in 1935, there were no Canadian authors or composers participating in or benefiting by the collections. This was the cause of some criticism. On the floor of this house some six months later it was revealed that there were only seven Canadian authors and composers. The directors of the American and English societies simply assigned to the new Canadian Performing Right Society copyrights to between 2,000,000 and 3,000.000 pieces of music. One might say that that is the stock-in-trade of the Canadian Performing Right Society. It is on these alleged copyrights that they proceed to collect fees from users of music throughout the dominion.
Who is there in the house who can say that the American and English companies had title to the copyrighted music transferred to Canada. Nobody knows whether they had title or not. They simply come in and tell the government that they have title to between
2.000,000 and 3.000.000 pieces of music, and under the statute they are authorized to issue licences and to collect fees in compensation for the use of the music. They have proceeded to collect their fees in a most arbitrary fashion, largely by threats. A bill may be presented to an applicant, and in the event of the applicant refusing to pay, or in the event of his using a piece of music on which they contend they have a copyright, legal action is suggested.
At present the Canadian Performing Right Society is the only company exercising the right to issue licences and to collect fees in Canada. But one cannot say how many more concerns may come in and claim the same right, provided they can show title to certain pieces of music. I do not think it would be difficult for them to show just as good title as the present Canadian Performing Right Society is able to show
My point is that thert is nothing to indicate that the society which collects the fees does have actual possession of or actual right to the copyrights in question, and there has never been any particular effort to make them prove their right. Under the statute they are compelled to register their titles in the copyright
office. Early in the period of their business operations when they were depositing between two and three million titles in the copyright office, they simply deposited whole catalogues showing various pieces of music. As recently as last year they have been known to attempt to collect fees on music to which they had absolutely no right or title. If this is done in one case it is fair to assume that it is done in others. Their fees until the appointment of the appeal board have certainly been varied, and subject to all sorts of combinations.
Since 1931, when they first attempted to collect fees they have filed no less than nine separate tariffs, each one of which had a tendency to increase rather than to reduce. The joker in the present tariffs is that everything is based upon a minimum and from the minimum there may be gradual increases by calculations and conditions until a maximum, the certainty of which can never be established, is reached. Between the minimum and the maximum they are on safe ground. It would appear, therefore, that the Canadian Performing Right Society is a very clear example of "heads I win, tails you lose."
Thus far they say they have deposited in the copyright office about 200,000 titles. The purpose of the amendment is to require the society in its collections to give to every user of music a list of the titles to which it claims ownership or upon which it claims authority to collect fees. That list should be certified by the Secretary of State. The excuse is made that this would involve an expenditure of $10,000 for printing. Let us assume that such is the case; that would simply be a capital expenditure on the part of a firm doing a very profitable business. This concern, under the 1937 tariff, collects
570.000	from the broadcasting stations of this dominion. Our own Canadian Broadcasting Corporation contributes $15,000 of this $70,000. Is there anyone in business w'ho has not to make some capital expenditure? A lawyer must buy his books, his office fixtures and so on, and a merchant must put up his shelving and counters, buy his stock and do his advertising. Those are capital expenditures which must be made. Why should not this performing right society expend $10,000 or $20,000 in order that the public may be protected?
We all admit the principle that an author or composer should be protected, that his rights should be secured, but the public generally is also entitled to protection. In addition to the 870,000 contributed by the broadcasting stations, the theatres of Canada pay
860.000	annually as fees t.o thw society. rrl,en

I ask hon. members if it is unreasonable to require that this performing right society shall give to every applicant for a licence a list of the music to which it claims to have the copyright and for which it claims authority to collect a fee? I am going to ask this house to give earnest and sympathetic consideration to these amendments which concern the protection of the public. When these people go out to collect licence fees they should be required to satisfy the applicant for a licence that they have ownership in that which they offer for sale. It is unfortunate that this whole matter is not of a more material nature. There is no reason why this society should not be paying a sales tax. There is no reason why they should not pay for the privileges they enjoy in this dominion.
They do not stop to consider for one moment how much of a drain the payment of a licence will be upon the resources of an applicant. If the applicant refuses to pay, he is told that they will bring action against him. I commend the minister for having set up an appeal board. This board is doing the best it can under the circumstances to carry out the provisions of the act. However, it is serving simply as a stop-gap in preventing the Canadian Performing Right Society from changing its tariffs two or three times a year.
The second amendment deals with the licence fees charged the smaller users of radios and an exemption is asked for these users. As I said before, under the 1937 tariff the broadcasting stations paid a total of $70,000, of which $15,000 was contributed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In addition to the broadcasting stations there are the little fellows, the skating rinks, the lodge halls, the hotels, the restaurants and so on that use radios for some purpose or other. We may have a restaurant with four or five tables on either side of an aisle with a little radio to provide music for the guests. Along comes a representative of the Canadian Performing Right Society who charges this man $5 as a minimum fee. He is then told he must make continuous and voluminous reports as to what music is played, how many hours per day and how many days per week the different pieces

are played. There are more reports to be made to this society than are necessary in making income tax returns to dominion, provincial and municipal governments. These small users of radios claim that they have paid for their radios, that they have paid the dominion government a fee of 82, and they want to know what use their radios will be if they cannot get music from the broadcasting stations without additional expense. I appeal again to hon. members to give sympathetic consideration to this bill. The amendments suggested therein affect every constituency in the dominion, no matter how large or how small it may be. I could not possibly read these amendments myself, so I ask the Clerk to be good enough to read them in order that the house may have a clear conception of their meaning.

Mr. Speaker, I wish first t,o congratulate the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) upon the sincerity of his purpose and upon the constant study he has given to copyright matters. The hon. member has participated in every debate which we have had on this question during a number of years, and has shown considerable moderation in the presentation of his views, which I must say I cannot altogether share. I hesitate to recommend the adoption of this bill. Perhaps I can put the position more clearly by saying that I cannot recommend its acceptance as I do not consider this to be the opportune moment to offer such amendments. The amendments themselves are not acceptable.
Last year the Copyright Act was amended very materially. All matters of copyright which concerned the Canadian Performing Right Society were inquired into by Judge Parker during 1935. His report was received after an exhaustive study had been made of the situation. The government last year brought down amendments to give effect to that report, and the amendments covered very fully the recommendations which were made by Judge Parker. Those amendments were submitted to the house and were adopted both in this house and in the other chamber. The bill went before a committee of the senate, and I remember that over there the senators recommended that a fair trial be given to the recommendations made by Judge Parker; that we should' let time prove to what extent they were desirable. I must repeat that both points which have been made by my hon. friend to-night and which

Copyright Amendment-Mr. Rinjret
are covered by his bill were very fully covered in the report of Judge Parker, and in both cases his conclusions were quite different from those at which my hon. friend has arrived.
As the house will remember, the bill that was put through last year provided for the appointment of an appeal board to which these question of the performing rights of musical compositions could be referred. The bill provided that the fees of the performing right society should be filed by the month of November, and if any objection were taken to them, those objections were to be referred to an appeal board. The appeal board, which was set up in December, is composed of Mr. Justice Maclean, a judge of the exchequer court, the under-secretary of state, Mr. Coleman, and a lawyer from the Department of Justice, Mr. Fontaine. The fees of the performing right society were published in the Canada Gazette of November 7; the board heard the objections to them and listened to representations from both sides, and on January 2 the Canada Gazette published the revised tariffs which are to prevail during the year 1937.
I appeal to the house:	After both chambers have approved the bill which provides for this tribunal to hear both sides and to act as arbitrators in the matter, and after the fees have already been arbitrated and are now officially in force for the year 1937, is it reasonable, only one month after this is done, to ask the House of Commons to amend the act further and to change the whole situation by act of parliament? I do not think it is. I think the least we can do is to let things go along as they stand and to watch the results of that arbitration, which was a compromise effort to bring together the representatives of the performers on the one side, and of the society, representing the composers, on the other.
I know there is in this house quite a considerable body of opinion that even as now existing the performing rights of the Canadian Performing Right Society are exacting. I say that purposely for, because of my own views and feelings on the matter and because of a desire for good will of the government, I resent very much the stand taken during last session by societies of authors and, composers who cursed the government and who directed against the member of the government in charge of this bill a certain, literature which was very unworthy and very unjust, when I do stand here in the honesty of my purpose to reach a compromise in this matter that will be fair to the composers, on the one hand, and to the performers and the public on the other.
With the discussion which took place last year,-and I must say in all fairness that it did take place somewhat late in the session and therefore perhaps did not afford the fullest expression of views from all corners of the house-I think the authors and composers must have felt that with the bill we did propose we were standing as a protection between them and the feelings of quite a number of hon. members representing the public in this country. But the house did give its confidence to the government; as I said, the bill was before a committee of the senate, and the senate took the attitude that it was worth while to try this experiment of having an arbitration exercised in this matter by the tribunal which I have just described.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that it is not opportune, now that these tariffs have been in force for only a few weeks, to ask the house further to amend the Copyright Act and to throw overboard all that we did last year.
I also wish, to say that notwithstanding that general view of the question, I cannot accept, at least for the present, either of the amendments which my hon. friend proposes in his bill. In the first section of his bill my hon. friend suggests that the performing right society should not only file a copy of its works with the department of the Secretary of State, but also, when a licence is applied for, furnish to each applicant a complete list of all the works so filed. That, at first sight, may appear to be a fair demand, but it is absolutely in contradiction to the very spirit of copyright. When a copyright is filed with us or when a patent is applied for or when a trade mark is asked, for, it is never stipulated that the owner of that copyright or patent or trade mark must supply the public with a description or a list of that thing, whatever it may be. Such a procedure, moreover, would not in the least apply in this specific case because here we are dealing with a society which controls the performances of practically all musical works of composers of the different countries of the world. It is because the society is of that kind that we maintained that we could control its prices notwithstanding the convention of Rome and the undertaking there given by Canada together with other countries. We have to deal with a very special case. We have to deal with a necessary monopoly, if I may put it in that way, and that is why we believe we are justified in having established a control of its tariffs. That is also a reason why we should not exact from the society, not merely the filing of all its musical compositions with the Department of the Secretary of State, but what my hon. friend further asks for, namely,

Copyright Amendment-Mr. Rinfret
that whenever a licence is applied for the society should furnish a complete list of its musical compositions. I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the number of these compositions runs into a million, and the senate last year amended the bill to make it read that only musical pieces in current use should be filed with my department. So, least of all, should my hon. friend ask that the act should be amended in such a way as to force that society to supply a complete list of its works to the public. I insist also that this is not practical. Inasmuch as the society collects a licence fee which covers all musical compositions, there is no practical use in any member of the public having a complete list because the licence covers them all. Dealing with that particular point, I might add that Judge Parker was very clear in his report that the filing of such a list was not practicable. Let me quote from his report at page 33 on the filing of lists. The judge said:
When it is shown by program analysis that of the 25,982 musical numbers performed in Canada in 1934 only 4.841 numbers were controlled by Performing Right Society and 4,370 numbers were controlled by all other European Societies, it seems absurd and significant that Canadian Performing Right Society should waste time and money on filing a list of the works that possibly never have been and never may be performed in Canada.
That is the statement made by the judge who inquired very fully into this situation. Therefore I say that it is neither practicable nor justifiable to ask from that society not only the filing of their lists with the department of the Secretary of State but the supplying of those lists-which would be voluminous and very costly-to all applicants for licences.
As to the second section of the bill of my hon. friend, I shall be very frank about it and say that some day may come when his wish will seem acceptable and when it will appear that we have reached the point which is dealt with in that section. But again I say I do not think it would be advisable to accept that amendment now. If the hon. member will refer to the terms of the convention of Rome, 1928, which is the amended convention of that of Berne, he will find that in article 13 this very point is covered. Let me read article 13 of the convention of Rome:
The authors of musical works shall have the exclusive right of authorizing (1) the adaptation of those works to instruments which can reproduce them mechanically; and (2) the public performance of the said works by means of these instruments.
I again point out No. 2, "The public performance of the said works by means of these instruments." This means the performance

of such works by a corporation or a radio operating in a public place, and that is exactly what is covered by what my hon. friend wants his amendment to strike out from our Copyright Act. The matter was dealt with by Judge Parker in his report, and if my hon. friend refers to it he will find that under different titles-page 34, concerning the broadcasting tariff; page 40, the hotel tariff; page 42, the parks, small fairs and community halls tariff; and page 43, restaurants, skating rinks, et cetera- Judge Parker has recommended a lower minimum than the one which was requested by the society. He has maintained the principle that these small places should pay at least a minimum licence fee, and that is what has been maintained by the appeal board, as will be seen if anybody refers to the tariff filed and published in the Canada Gazette of January 2.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think we should avoid bringing in this year further amendments to the Copyright Act, and should especially avoid these amendments, because they have been dealt with by the judge, by the house, by the senate and by the appeal board, and in every case a decision has been arrived at which is totally different from the one that is proposed in this bill.
In conclusion I may say I know that the Copyright Act, like any other act, is perfectible, and I know by my own experience with these matters-and it has not been very pleasant all the time-that there exists a great difference of view in this country about copyright. At the same time I believe we have gone as far as possible to meet the desires of the public and to curb the activities of the Canadian Performing Right Society, and by going further at present we would risk ignoring the rights of the owners themselves, who after all also deserve consideration.
As I say, the new tariff has been in force for only one month; the appeal court sat about five or six weeks ago, and it would be a great mistake not to allow several months to pass and permit this new experiment, this new arbitration, to work itself for the time being. Therefore, while not compromising any future consideration that we may have of the act, I cannot see my way clear to accepting the bill as it is, and I shall have to recommend to the house not to pass its second reading.
May I add that there should have been an international conference in Brussels last fall. For several reasons it unfortunately did not take place, but it is contemplated that the various nations which were parties to the conventions of Berne and Rome will meet either this fall or perhaps in the spring of

Copyright Amendment-Mr. Neill
1938. This, I believe, is a further reason why we should not disturb the amendments that we have brought to the act in the course of the last session.

I am sorry that the minister has announced his intention of declaring "thumbs down" on this bill, and particularly so at this stage, before he allowed the ordinary members of the house, other than the introducer, any opportunity to express their views. It is customary, I think, to hear what may be said by the various members and for the government, ostensibly at least, to sum up the situation and announce their decision. In this case the decision has been given first. Nevertheless I feel impelled by the interests that my constituents and I have in this matter to support the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling), and I congratulate him upon the attitude he has taken and the very able manner in which he has expressed himself.
Dealing with the remarks of the minister, I believe he took a somewhat different view of the bill from that which is justified by its terms. The minister said or suggested that the hon. member was trying to change the whole set-up of the radio act. I do not think a consideration of the bill bears out that statement. There is no suggestion of material change, and certainly there is no suggestion and no attempt to change the arbitration features of it which were in the good act which the minister introduced last year, and which were a very good thing indeed. The bill does not in any way interfere with them.
The minister talks about the amendments not being opportune, and says that we are proposing to amend a bill which was introduced or passed only last year. It is always opportune to correct a grievance or an error, and I think the history of parliamentary practice and of legislation will show that it is quite a common thing to amend an act a year after it has been passed because experience has shown a need for amendment. I imagine that was the motive of the hon. member for Kootenay West in bringing in this bill. My personal complaint would rather be, not altogether as to the charges that have been proposed there, but as to the method of computing them, and I shall deal with that a little later on.
The hon. member for Kootenay West, as he stated, asks two things. He suggests that the company should give out a list of all articles or songs or music over which they claim the exclusive control. I do not think that is unreasonable. When the agent of the
company comes around to these small people and says " I want to collect so much from you," and the man says, "What is it for?" and the agent says, " Why, you are using or you are going to use articles or music of which we have the sole control," I do not think it is unreasonable for the man to say, " Well, show me your authority or show me your ownership."
As regards the alleged enormous cost of printing these titles, I suppose this would be only the titles of these various songs or pieces of music. It is surely not unreasonable to suppose that this company, who claim that they own them and have obtained the exclusive copyright in them or had it assigned to them, have a list of what they possess, and if they have it, the actual cost of printing it would be very small indeed. They claim that they have had this copyright assigned to them in many cases, I think, and that they collect these charges and allocate them or at least a portion of them to the authors. How are they going to know where the authors are, or who they are, or what they shall allocate to them if they have not a list? I do not think the company themselves would dare to say that they have not a complete list of all the articles over which they have jurisdiction, and if that is so, the cost of reprinting the list would be trivial. Otherwise it leaves the door open for the company to come forward and make a claim to ownership of articles and music to which they have no right, and we are utterly helpless and in their hands and are obliged to pay up, in total ignorance as to whether they have the least elemental right to some of the things over which they claim jurisdiction. Surely it ought to be open to any man running some small place such as a restaurant to say, " I will not use any of the music over which you claim to have jurisdiction, any music to which you claim sole rights, but you tell me exactly what those are and I will make use of the others." But, no. The agent simply comes along and says, "We claim jurisdiction over practically everything that is printed," and the man has to pay.
The bill proposes to do away with charges for the use of radios or gramophones in certain hotels, public halls and stores, but it does not apply to theatres or other such places; it is only the smaller halls, restaurants, stores and so on. As the hon. member who introduced this bill points out, the radio broadcasting stations pay 870,000 to this copyright society-some people would' call it a racketeering society. This is supposed to cover compensation for private and domestic use only.
492	COMMONS
Copyright Amendment-Mr. Neill
The purpose of the bill is to make it cover also the use of music in small stores or halls, hotels, skating rinks and the like.
I would call attention to the method by which these charges are computed and ask hon. members whether they think it reasonable or conducive to the ordinary running of a business. I am not referring now to the big departmental houses that can afford to employ lawyers, statisticians and mathematicians to calculate the fees; I am referring to the man who runs a small business such as a hotel, a pool-room, a Greek restaurant, or a barber shop. One of these agents will come along and, as the hon. member has said, use strong-arm methods. He will say, "We want to collect SIS from you"; the pool-room man will reply that only a short time ago he paid S25, and he will ask what the extra charge is lor. The agent replies, "Never mind what it is for; these are the charges; you can calculate them for yourself, and if you don't pay up you will be prosecuted," and he immediately produces a list of successful prosecutions. They have always been successful in their prosecutions, because in days gone by they had an iron-clad law behind them, and they would threaten'-the hon. member for Kootenay West was justified in using that word- about what would be done if the victim did not pay up at once. This small man is perhaps not too familiar with the English language, or too well educated, even if he should happen to be of British birth; how then is he to cope with a situation such as this?
I propose to read to the house the method by which the charge is arrived at. This is in connection with halls, restaurants, skating rinks and stores, and it gives the fees "on maximum basis," whatever that may be. On that basis the rates are so much. These are not maximum charges but charges on maximum basis, and further on it deals with charges "on actual basis." There is always a minimum fee to begin with. What I shall read consists of 144 words and it is all one sentence. There are only a few commas in it and I shall indicate them, so that I may not be accused of trying to make it out to be worse than it is. After I have read it through, if any hon. member can assure me that he understands it I shall sit down and make no further objection to this racket. The clause reads:
The rate is one and one-half cents for each "performer hour" for a licence covering the maximum number of "performer hours," the maximum of "performer hours" being determined by multiplying the maximum number of performers (including musicians, orchestra leader and vocalists) that may be employed at any time during the licence year by the

maximum number of hours of all or any musical performance during which is desired a licence to perform in any day during the licence year wholly or in part from the society's repertoire, by the maximum number of days for which a licence is desired in any week in the licence year, by the same number as the number of weeks occurring between the opening and closing dates of the period of time within which musical performances may take place, but in no case by a number less than thirteen (weeks).
Does anyone know what figure is charged there? Some suspicion of this question seems to have dawned on the man who drafted it because he goes on to say what the actual basis is. What I have just read is the maximum basis, but on actual basis the rate is as follows:
The rate is three cents for each "performer hour" for a licence covering all actual hours of musical performance during the licence year.
A payment is required on account and in advance equal to the amount due at the above rate on the total "performer hours" as estimated by the applicant, the advance payment to be not less than $5.
The licensee is required to report, at the end of the licence year or of each operating season within the licence year, the actual number of "performer hours" during such period, giving dates and times of all musical performances and the number of performers engaged thereat, the licensee at such times to make payment of any balance due.
Next we came to hotels:
The fee payable is determined as follows:
(1)	An initial payment is required annually in advance in an amount calculated at the rate of 10 cents per room charged on the total room capacity of the hotel, the minimum initial payment being $15.
(2)	At the end of each quarter an additional payment is required in an amount determined by multiplying the number of rooms in the hotel by the units of performance, by the number of months within which music is at times performed, by the rate (1 cent or less).
This is not quite clear and so the draftsman undertakes to explain it:
The rate is determined as follows:
If the hotel's average daily occupancy in the months within which music is at times performed is 80 per cent or over, the rate is 1 cent. If occupancy falls below 80 per cent, the rate is 1 cent less a deduction of 2 per cent thereof for each 1 per cent that occupancy falls below 80 per cent.
This is as clear as mud; the barman or the man who cleans boots could figure it out.
What is the hon. member quoting from? Has it been approved by the department?
Yes; it is from the Canada Gazette of January 2.

One can hardly believe it.

Copyright Amendment-Mr. Lockhart

But the worst is yet to come. Let us see what "units of performance" are:
Units
Music at lunch time (12 noon to 2 p.m.)	 2
Music at tea time (2 p.m. to 5 p.m.)..	2
Music at dinner time (5 p.m. to 8 p.m.).	2
And so on. Payments are made on as high as ten units. The following example is given:
An hotel having 250 rooms-initial payment	 $25
On 4 units of performance during only 2 months of the quarter, the average daily occupancy being 70 per cent during the 2 months-additional quarterly fee (250 x 4 x 2 x -8 cents)	 $16
It works out that it is $16. I would rather pay the $16 than go through the calculation.
That, then, is what one would call the fundamental charge, then there are extras. If a hotel has a radio in a public room there is an extra charge for the number of bedrooms. Then there is a charge for an occasional entertainment, or for a single entertainment. If that does not lend itself to unhindered extortion I do not know what does. Of course it is useless to argue, because the minister has given his ultimatum. I can only say that a great many people in Canada think of this society as the hon. member for Kootenay West and I do, that it is a racket.
Hear, hear.

May I add a word in regard to the interpretation of this law? It has been my experience to follow very closely the application of this act to benevolent societies and fraternal and friendly organizations. I shall cite a particular instance, relating to a building in which I am interested as chairman of the trustee board. The inspector of the society attended a gathering there as a detective and then wrote a letter stating definitely that the program included four items subject to fees. When a request was sent in to get a list of the protected numbers, the answer came back from the society that they did not furnish lists. I contend that fraternal organizations which during the past five years have been making an earnest effort to raise funds to take care of less fortunate members should at least have the protection of being provided with a list of numbers which they may not play unless they pay a licence fee. I know many hon. members have had experiences similar to mine in this matter. Fraternal organizations, church societies and similar groups, which have been trying to raise money to distribute to less
fortunate people, find themselves compelled to pay these fees. The society should at least be required to provide a list of its protected works; then it would be easy for small groups, where the orchestra may consist of only a piano and two other instruments, to avoid playing numbers licensed by this society. These small organizations, carrying on useful social and benevolent and fraternal work in this country, should have that protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIRS OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: That is quite correct. Loans are reported to the department after they are made. The department examines the forms provided for the purpose in order to see that the loans have been made under the conditions prescribed by the regulations and the act. If, in the opinion of the department, a loan does not come within that category, the bank or lending institution will be in the position of having made a loan without having a government guarantee with respect to it.

subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIRS OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext: Supposing someone asks for a loan and is refused; can he go to his member to ask for a recommendation that such loan be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIRS OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
I must point out that the discretion with respect to the credit of the individual applying for a loan is with the lending institutions. We have attempted to eliminate a great deal of the red tape associated with small loans and have prescribed the limit of discount which may be charged. There must be no endorser or other collateral asked for; it must be a loan upon the personal credit of the individual. We do not take any steps to influence a bank to lend to one man or to another; the bank must be the judge of the individual's credit standing. I know of nothing which would be a surer way of involving the full guarantee of the dominion than to create a situation whereby pressure could be brought to bear upon the lending institution to make loans in particular cases. I think that would be very bad for the plan. The criticism with respect to this might be that the banks may not be reasonably sympathetic. I may point out that committees are to be formed in local communities all over Canada. If, because of some technicality, a bank is unable to grant a loan, it will be the duty of the committee to investigate the case and, if possible, to adjust the technicalities in order that the loan may be made.
I cannot make it too clear that the lending institution must be the judge of the character of the applicant. We cannot pretend to set up, in connection with the hundreds of thousands of loans which we hope and believe will be made under this law, machinery whereby the government could insist upon, a loan being made to John Jones or William Smith. Certainly if a complaint is received by the department that a branch of a bank is adopting an arbitrary attitude or is unwilling to proceed in accordance with the legislation, the department will take up the matter and ask for an explanation as to why cooperation is not forthcoming from this branch as it is from others. I think to ask the department
to interfere with respect to particular cases, to insist upon a loan being granted to a particular individual, would defeat one of the major purposes of the bill. I may say I have had no complaint in that regard during the period which has elapsed since the plan has been in force.

Yes, and that there is nothing wrong so far as the lending of the money is concerned, that more is not being charged by certain corporations which shall be designated as lending corporations. Certain organizations might be lending corporations and be supplying materials too, and they should not be allowed to overcharge their customers for the materials used. Is any power granted to them to exercise a certain amount of supervision, or is a person who is seeking to borrow money compelled to bring in some form of document to show how the money is going to be used? I make this suggestion because in the past I have had a little experience in housing operations, and I know something of how money has been spent, even squandered at times, after it has been lent. I know the difficulty which provincial governments have today in repaying money that was borrowed under the housing act of 1919 just because of lack of supervision at that time. This time I hope, whether it is a federal housing act 
or an act for the purposes of rehabilitation, that proper supervision will be exercised to see that the money is spent properly and to the advantage of the individual concerned and the country as a whole.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the discussion before the dinner recess the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) asked a question of the minister relative to what was a home, and he furnished the reply that in the rural areas a home included any bams and outbuildings of various kinds. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION TO ENCOURAGE REPAIRS OF RURAL AND URBAN DWELLINGS
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, in our first draft of the legislation we attempted to arrive at more specific definitions, but as the work went on for the first two months the differences which arose between localities caused us constantly to consider widening the definition of a home. If my hon. friend will look forward to section 8, paragraph (e), he will find that provision is made for regulations in regard to the definition of rural and urban homes:
" Rural and urban homes," with power to include in such expression all such property as may reasonably be considered as part of a rural or urban home.
I thought that the committee might reasonably want to have that more closely defined, but I frankly confess that I had some difficulty with regard to it in actual operation. For instance, there had to be a regulation with regard to new houses that a man had built but had not quite finished. Should we deal with those? There had also to be regulations with respect to the inclusion of certain buildings with a farm house. Shall a barn or a garage be included? Shall a summer cottage be eligible? Then, with regard to combined stores and dwellings, we had to evolve a regulation to provide that the plan would not be abused by being used for commercial rather than dwelling purposes. That is a matter of some difficulty, as my hon. friend will understand. Tourist cabins-there was a thorny question.

I could go on over a couple of pages instancing the degrees of variation which arise, and which caused me finally to decide to recommend to the committee that we be given power by regulation to make definitions subject to that qualification I have just quoted, "which may reasonably be considered as part of a rural or urban home." On consideration I felt that that was the best solution.
With respect to the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), I am afraid we are rather at cross-purposes. He speaks of the necessity for supervision in order to see that the money is spent for the purpose for which it is loaned. Well, Mr. Chairman, if this plan is to succeed in its major objective, which is to create work by encouraging people to do hundreds of thousands of small jobs, effectively to follow the money to its ultimate spending by the individual who borrows it in small amounts is virtually impossible, and I believe it would be regarded by borrowers generally of small sums of from one to three hundred dollars as more of what is generally described as governmental red tape. Only this afternoon I had a criticism from a member about what? About the information demanded of a man before he could get a loan. You see, we get it coming and going. In the one case we have not enough supervision, and in the other the criticism is that we have too much. I would point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who I know is desirous of assisting, not of blocking, the plan, that the application for a home improvement loan must be made on a form approved by the department, and it is the only form the use of which properly filled out will qualify the lending institution to get the government guarantee with respect to the amount loaned in the particular case. That form asks for a complete description of the repairs intended, along with much other information-my hon. friend criticized the amount of information asked for-and it winds up by saying-this is the borrower authorizing the lender:
I authorize you to obtain such information as you may require concerning the above statement, and agree that it shall remain your property whether or not my note is finally accepted by you. I certify that if the loan is granted to me the entire proceeds will be used exclusively in payment for alterations, repairs and/or improvements on the property described above. I hereby affirm that the foregoing information is true and correct.
That is what the borrower says. When this form goes to the department, there is a certificate from the manager of the branch bank advancing the money:
I certify that this day a loan for $	
for	 months repayable in	
instalments, was made to the above mentioned applicant for the purpose named by negotiating
his note for $	less discount of $	
calculated in accordance with the official tables, and having scrutinized and checked this application with the care ordinarily required of me by the bank, I certify to the best of my knowledge that the conditions and purpose of this loan are such as qualify it for the dominion government guarantee under the home improvement plan.
That is signed then by the bank manager. The information which appears on the form, the affirmation of the borrower, represents the distance which we believe we should go in creating red tape in the form of supervision around the expenditure of this money. After all, the people who will be borrowing this money are not well-off people. It is a loan. It must be paid back. Community interest in the plan involves that a considerable number of people will know what is going on, and I think in that widespread publicity and in the community nature of the enterprise rests our major protection against wrongful use of the money, together, of course, with the affirmation and with the penalty further on in the bill with regard to misrepresentation and obtaining a loan not in accordance with the provisions.

speechtext: The minister may be interested to know that the case I had in mind was that of one of my constituents who wanted to put a portable garage behind his house. speechtext: I should appreciate a further explanation from the minister as to the test to be applied to determine whether an applicant is credit-worthy, to use the term the minister himself used. It is very difficult for me to answer in specific terms, because, as my hon. friend knows, credit is something that belongs to a man's own self and to the conditions under which he lives and under which he receives his income. I know of cases in which loans have been made where the income is seasonal, as in farming or fishing, but I could not attempt to lay down any specific rule to determine the creditworthiness of an individual except to say this. Generally speaking, I am advised that these loans are being approached on the basis of character. But of course, even with respect to a man of good character, the lender is not doing a service to that individual by lending him something which it is quite apparent, from the man's circumstances and his prospective income, he cannot repay. All these considerations must enter into the determination of the question whether or not an individual loan should be made. I am sure that my hon. friend, who is familiar with the middle west, as I am, will acknowledge that many of us out there were considered more credit-worthy during one period of the history of the west
at any rate than we turned out to be, and even some of my hon. friends from Toronto have had that experience as well as those of us from the west.

speechtext: It would depend upon the lender; a particular lender might consider a man credit-worthy. Suppose a banker in Fort William were asked for a loan; he might be more willing to lend than a banker in Toronto. He might be more generous in a particular case. Any banker in the community, before he lends his money, will be sure that the borrower is worthy and that the loan will be of service to him.

There is an increase of $35,000 in, this item. Will the minister give a general outline to show whether the increase is caused merely by the normal advancement of civil service salaries or whether there are special items contributing to it.

The hon. member will note that on the whole item the increase is not $35,000 but the difference between $30,285 and $35,000, or a net increase of $4,715. The increase is arrived at in this way. There is a decrease in salaries amounting to $30,285. This is due to the abolition of fourteen positions not further required, amounting to $19,435, and to the fact that twenty-five positions are occupied by temporary employees who were not made permanent as expected and whose salaries, amounting to $26,195, are provided for in the contingency item. In addition to those two sums there is a net saving, by the promotion of officers at lower salaries than those paid to their predecessors, of $6,405. The total of the three sums I have mentioned is $52,035, against which one must place statutory increases amounting to $21,750, leaving a net decrease in the

salary item of $30,285. Now I come to the increase in the contingency item. The increase in this item amounting to $35,000 is due to the transfer of the salaries of twenty-five temporary employees from the permanent vote, amounting to $26,195, plus $8,805 to provide a safe margin for future requirements.

The minister has me confused in a mass of figures. Are the detailed items included in item 14 on page 7 those set out in detail on page 83 of this year's estimates? If so, I wish to call something to his attention in connection with some details, in order to save my raising the point on each item.
The answer is yes.

Thank you. In the estimates of 1936-37 which were before us last session, in several individual instances very substantial increases were shown over the previous year. If my recollection serves me aright, the minister explained those increases last year as being due to increased staff required to handle matters in the department. This year the minister in his estimates shows a decrease over last year, but a large increase over the year before, indicating that last year in the estimates he showed large increases which apparently were never required and never used. For example, take item 17 of the 1936-37 estimates, on page 83 of this year's estimates. This year it is shown as $49,080 as against $48,000 last year. The same item in the estimates of 1936-37 which were before us last session showed the estimated expenditure as $51,0000, as against $47,100 for the year before. The net result is that last year's estimates showed a very substantial increase, whereas this year it shows a decrease, but in reality there has been a steady increase in the item each year since this government has been in power. And I have picked only one item out of seven or eight which I could enumerate in this year's estimates. I should like to know what was the scheme or idea of inserting in last year's estimates vast increases which obviously were never required. Was it in order that this year the estimates might show a decrease?
Probably I should call the minister's attention to item 65 of last year's estimates- because it was the outstanding one- which would be item 52 in this year's, shown on page 83. This year the estimate shows $69,930. In the outside column it shows that last year there was voted $82,620. Therefore the minister says there is a decrease of approximately $13,000. On the other hand, if we take exactly the same item in last year's estimates,
[Mr. Ilsley.J
we find that last year it was increased from $63,000 to $82,620. I should like to know the explanation of that amazing apparent juggling of figures.
I am unable to appreciate my hon. friend's adjectives, if he will pardon my saying so. The terms "vast" and "amazing" do not apply to these minor changes.
The sum of $13,000 is hardly minor.

The first item my hon. friend pointed out is the one referring to head clerks, where the difference is between $48,000 for 1936-37 and $49,080 for 1937-38. I assume that difference would be due to statutory increases. As to the other item which my hon. friend mentioned, it is not correct to refer to that as item 52. The word "number" at the top of the left hand columns on page 83 relates to the number of persons employed. The number employed in 1936-37 was sixty-five, and for 1937-38 the estimated number is fifty-two. We apparently have been able to cut down somewhat on the staff, either that or they are in the temporary class instead of permanent. I think the latter is the proper explanation.
May I interrupt to make my point clear? If the minister will be good enough to look at last year's estimates-
I do not have them before me.

Well, if he will accept my word that in the column of numbers in 1935-36 there were shown forty-nine persons employed, he now submits an estimate for sixty-five persons for this year, and asks for an increase from $63,000 to $82,620, or, in other words, an increase of $19,620. But according to the estimates submitted this year the committee and the country would be led to believe that the number of employees in that branch had been curtailed from sixty-five last year to fifty-two this year with a corresponding reduction of $13,000 in salaries.

I may correct any erroneous impression the country might get on that point. Last year there were forty-nine stenographers, and they were permanent. It was expected, no doubt, that the number of permanents would be increased to sixty-five, but it was not deemed advisable, nor was it possible, to make them permanent, and so the number of permanents is only fifty-two, substantially what it was last year.

Yes, a little bit over.
Does item No. 14 include customs appraisers?
Only those at head office.

Who is responsible for the regulations under which appraisals are made? Is it the minister, or are there certain officials in the department who advise the minister? Perhaps I can make myself clear in this way:	I believe somewhere in a discussion of the estimates a question should be asked as to the regulations which have been made in the past year with respect to the S100 tourist exemption. When parliament prorogued, certain exemptions had been made, and following the prorogation of parliament apparently a number of regulations were issued to officials at customs offices. In many instances the regulations seemed to limit or to abolish the exemption.
For example, I have in mind regulations laid down in connection with radios. One could bring in a radio in his car, but could not bring in a radio attached to his automobile. I heard of an instance of a car coming into Canada with four new tires bought in the United States. The owner who crossed on the boat from Seattle to Vancouver or Victoria was warned that if the tires were on the car they were dutiable, but if they were off the car they could enter duty free. He took the tires off, ran the ear in on the rims and brought the tires in duty free. May I add I was told, that by an officer of the department. If such things can happen, then I say the provision in the budget has been made ridiculous by departmental regulations.
I have been looking for an item under which the matter may be discussed, and I thought this might be the proper place to do so. I 'have in mind difficulties which have arisen in Calgary and elsewhere in connection with persons who have imported radios and then have found themselves in the position of being liable to attack for the violation of certain patents. One point which seems to puzzle people in Canada, myself included, is how the companies concerned with the
patents know, without access to or advice from the department, that an individual has imported a radio containing tubes which infringe patent regulations. Reviewing three or four striking cases which have been brought to my attention I believe the intention of parliament has been largely nullified by regulations which have been laid diown. Either the exemption is good or it is not good. I think these facts should be brought to the attention of the minister and the officials with him so that through the minister they may be able to advise the committee as to the regulations which have been made.

Before I say what I 'have in mind, may I read tariff item 703 (b) which states that the following goods are free under all tariffs.
(b) Goods valued at not more than one hundred dollars included in the baggage accompanying residents of Canada returning from abroad after an absence from Canada of not less than forty-eight hours and acquired by them for personal or household use or as souvenirs or gifts, but not bought on commission or as an accommodation for other persons or for sale, under regulations prescribed by the minister.
Then follows a proviso. The words to which I would draw the attention of the hon. member are these: "Included an the baggage accompanying residents of Canada returning from abroad." I am quite free to admit that the department has experienced difficulty with these words and has received quite a number of complaints from residents of Canada returning from abroad. Almost entirely their complaints have been limited to the two matters mentioned by the hon. member, namely radios installed in cars and tires mounted on the wheels of cars coming into Canada.
The view taken by the department and by myself was that unless we depart entirely from the language of the item, as the Department of National Revenue we cannot possibly declare that automobile tires on wheels, revolving and in use when they come into Canada, are goods "included in the baggage accompanying residents of Canada returning from abroad." Similarly the department has said, and I agree, that we cannot rule that a radio affixed to a car as part of it, used in the car abroad, and actually brought back into Canada as part of the car, could be described as goods "included in the baggage of the resident returning to Canada."

But if he detached it
and put it into his trunk, it would be.

Yes. We have tried to give this a rather liberal interpretation-
Supply-National Revenue
Conservative.

The hon. member will bear in- mind that the Department of National Revenue is an administrative department. We have to carry out the will of parliament as expressed in the items we are administering. Otherwise we would be making administrative law, rather than carrying out the will of parliament. We have gone so far as to say that if the returning resident brings back a radio sitting loosely in the back seat of his car we shall regard it as baggage. Further, we have gone so far as to say that if he brings tires back he may carry them with him or have them loosely in the back seat of his car and we shall regard them as baggage. But when they are part of the car we cannot say, without departing from the language of the section, they are part of his baggage. These are the reasons for the rulings which have been made. Whether or not there should be a change in the wording of the item, I cannot say; at present we are not concerned with that.
It is very unsafe for an administrative department to depart from the undoubted meaning of the language. If we did so it would be subversive of law.
I can understand that, but I am pointing out what is a ridiculous state of affairs.
That may be.

A man may import four new tires into Canada if he carries them in on the back seat of his car. But if he has a blow-out in the United States, is forced to buy a new tire and run his car into Canada on that tire, it is classed as a new tire attached to the car, and he is liable to duty on it.
He always was.
With regard to the last suggestion of the hon. member, that owners of patents have access to the files of the department, I want to say that such is not the fact.
I am glad to have that assurance.

They have no such access and if an application was made for any information, it would be refused. It has always been the law that a person importing a
patented article for use or sale is liable to action. It has, however, never been part of the functions of the customs authorities to advise importers as to whether or not the importation of any article violates a patent. That -is something upon which we are not qualified to advise.
How do they get to know about it?
Second sight.

I do not know how patent owners learn that their patents are being infringed by importers, but I can think of many ways in which they might find out. Not long ago I heard of an instance where an exporter in the United States was advertising extensively that he was selling a certain patented article to Canadians. The owner of the patent in Canada immediately looked around to see where these were coming from, and I believe he started an action against some people.
Very frequently importers tell others how cheaply they were able to buy an article in the United States and thus give themselves away.

My recollection is that
there is a provision in the act permitting the inspection of invoice entries on payment of a nominal fee.
That is not available to anybody.
No stranger.
It is limited to the importer?
Yes.

I should think it would be possible for the Minister of National Revenue to place a less liberal interpretation upon the section to which reference has just been made.

Supply-National Revenue
If my recollection serves me correctly, the debate which took place in this house on that particular item was not such as to justify the minister and his department in taking such a liberal view of importations of this kind. If the minister would allow his Scotch instinct to prevail, this ultra liberal view would not be in force in the department. Canadian tradesmen ought to be given a little consideration. I hardly think the person who signed the treaty with the United States republic in which this clause was embodied, anticipated an interpretation of this sort. If the minister were an ordinary layman travelling back and forth between the United States and Canada, he would realize how ridiculous is this interpretation. It seems ridiculous when a man has to take a radio off his car, put it in the back seat until he gets past the customs and then attach it again to his car in order to comply with the interpretation of the regulation.
In order to get by.

We should interpret this regulation somewhat differently. While I am on my feet I should like to direct the attention of the minister to another matter in connection with his department. I have found the officials of his department to be extraordinarily capable, but I have also found that they are housed in an extraordinary manner. It is a real shame to expect capable officials to carry on their duties under such conditions as prevail at present in the department. There is one office which I visit quite frequently in which are located six men. On a recent visit to this office I found each of these six men trying to interview another man. The office was so littered with papers that one could hardly step from one desk to the next, and yet all these papers were necessary to the work of the department. The minister should give some consideration to the people in his department who are doing such efficient work. The conditions under which these people work should be improved. This would create a better impression in the minds of the public who visit these offices from time to time. Perhaps a better distribution of the space available would bring about the necessary results. It is awkward for someone trying to get information from an official to have five other officials giving information to five other individuals in the same office.

I appreciate the force of what my hon. friend has said. I am glad to join with him in paying a tribute to the officers of the department. I agree with his
statement as to their capability and competence, and I agree also as to the necessity for some improvement in office space. That matter is being considered at the present time and plans are being matured.

I should like to know what interpretation the minister places upon baggage contained in a car. Would that be hand baggage? I suppose many hon. members receive complaints in connection with this particular regulation. I had one incident brought to my attention of a man who had visited the United States where he had seen an oil stove of a type not possible to obtain in Canada. This was priced at about $80 and he thought he could bring it in. He had it crated and put into his car, but when he arrived at the port of entry he was assessed the regular duty. I understand the officer explained to him that if it had been a small parcel with a rope on it, something that he could carry, it would have been classed as baggage, but that the crate could not be thus classified. It is a question of baggage. I thought perhaps a large trunk would be considered as baggage. This is no bigger than a trunk.

The department takes the commonly accepted railway interpretation of baggage, what a passenger travelling on a railway train might be able to check as baggage or carry with him into a Pullman car. It may be that there is some variety of interpretation by different collectors because it is difficult to make a thoroughly consistent application of a rule such as that. It must be borne in mind that the past year is the first one during which this item has been in force, and it may be that certain collectors have taken one view and other collectors a different view, but the rule I have just mentioned is the rule of the department, which we follow very closely.

I agree from what I have heard that the interpretation is not uniform, because the gentleman informed me that if he had gone through another port he would have got through all right; that is, if he had understood before he came back that his own interpretation was wrong. As it was, he had to pay S31 or S32 duty on the stuff.

I really cannot let this item pass without congratulating the minister upon one subitem in it. Certainly.

Under date of March 18, 1930, Mr. Charles S. Cave, at that time a customs excise examiner on the staff at Halifax, made application for transfer to the port of Toronto in view of the health of his family since the Halifax explosion. I want to say that no private institution would treat any employee as Mr. Cave has been treated. I do not blame the department particularly. Perhaps it is because of some regulations that nothing has been done, but certainly something should be done to right a very great wrong. Mr. Cave says:
At the time of the Halifax disaster I was on duty (customs) at the Halifax graving docks, close to the point where the Mont Blanc blew up. I was blown into the Halifax harbour and my house, not far away, was blown off the map, three of my children were burned to death, and my wife and only surviving daughter were taken to Truro in a very serious condition. My wife has never fully recovered and for several years was under the doctor's care. I was advised by him that we would have to move elsewhere for her health's sake, so we decided to move to Toronto where her only surviving relatives were located.
Now it appears that he could not be transferred to Toronto, and later on, as I said a moment ago, he resigned from the department, but on the assumption that at a later date he would receive an appointment at Toronto. On various occasions he applied to the civil service commission for an appointment, and finally he was turned down because he was slightly over the age limit.
I want to compliment one official of the department, Mr. C. E. Wood, Commissioner of Customs, upon his humanitarian view of this case. In writing to the civil service commission, perhaps at the instance of the minister himself with whom I took this matter up a year ago, Mr. Wood says:
In view of the extenuating circumstances of which the department was not fully cognizant at the time, also the fact that while employed at Halifax, Mr. Cave's services were of the highest order, it would be appreciated if some way could be found to facilitate his re-entry to the customs excise service, notwithstanding that he now appears over the age limit.

The department also states that through his many years of service at Halifax Mr. Cave rendered excellent and efficient service, without any complaint at any time being made against him. I do hope that something will be done to give some consideration to this man who, while he was in the service of the government, lost his whole family but one through no fault of his own. It does seem to me, as one who has had a great deal to do with the employment of labour and who knows how labour should be treated, that a government official should not be treated as this man has been, and I would ask the minister to reconsider this case so that this man may be reemployed. Scores of officials have been appointed in Toronto since I brought this matter up, and surely this man can be put into some position.

The appointments to Toronto
have been made by the civil service commission, and my recollection is that when we took this matter up with the commission we were told that it was impossible to do anything for this man. Does the hon. member know the age of the man in question?
No, but I know he is a comparatively young man.
How long had he been in the service?
Twenty odd years. He is over the age required by the Civil Service Act.
He was with the department for many years and gave excellent service. It appears now that he is slightly over the age limit.
What is the age limit?
Thirty-five.

I think in view of the circumstances, when a man while in the service of the government had his house blown away at the time of that terrible disaster at Halifax, had three of his children burned to death and his wife left naturally in a state of collapse, and found it necessary, after struggling on for years at Halifax, to move away to some other part of the country, as any man would do under those circumstances even if he lost his position, something should be done for him. I do not believe any private company with branches scattered throughout Canada would have treated an employee in the way in which this gentleman has been treated.

There are several cases of this kind arising from time to time in various departments of the public service. The

Supply-Post Office
mistake in this case arose with the gentleman resigning. Once he resigned there is no power in the statute for anybody to place him in the public service again if he is over the age of thirty-five years, and the civil service commission could no more place him in a position than they could me. But there is a way in which the minister can deal with it if he so desires, and that is by placing an item in the supplementary estimates providing for the man's appointment notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act. In view of the circumstances to which reference has been made, and the letter written by a departmental official pointing out that all the facts were not in the possession of the department at the time this man felt compelled to resign in order to remove to another place where his wife could live, I would suggest that what I have indicated might be a very reasonable thing to do. This has been done more than once, and the only way in which it can be done is by act of parliament, because the statutory prohibition is such that he cannot otherwise be employed legally. The only way by which he can be legally employed is under a supplementary estimate, which of course is an act of parliament.
What is the total value of the imports under the S100 exemption?

Has the minister that by classification?

From the United States: automobile accessories, S100,826; automobile tires and tubes, S48.968; boots and shoes, $285,091; clothing, $1,455,924; foodstuffs, $11,702; furniture and household appliances, $442,004; miscellaneous commodities, $578,176, making the total previously mentioned of $2,931,691.
The totals from all countries are: automobile accessories, $100,871; automobile tires and tubes, $49,002; boots and shoes, $303,959; clothing, $1,755,013; foodstuffs, $15,207; furniture and household appliances, $467,529; miscellaneous commodities, $837,058, making a total I mentioned of $3,528,639.
What was the total of clothing and boots and shoes, the two important items?
From all countries?
The importations under this $100 exemption from all countries.
Boots and shoes, $303,959; clothing, $1,755,013.
Did the minister stop to think of how much labour that is depriving the people of Canada?
Out of order.

Before this item carries, I think the minister ought to deal a little more definitely with the case raised by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). If the department desire, ways and means can be found to have that man reestablished in his duties, around Toronto. Could he not at least be placed in temporary employment?
He cannot be placed in the service at all.

I think the minister spoke the other evening of a large number of appointments to the stenographic staff. If there is any way of having a special item in the estimates to meet his case or of placing him in the temporary service, I believe the government should do what any ordinary employer in Canada would do-transfer him from the employment in which he was formerly engaged to a place where he can find more congenial surroundings than in the place he left, namely the city of Halifax.

I am informed that this officer did not leave the service until thirteen years after the explosion. The explosion occurred in 1917, and this officer left the service in 1930; that may have some bearing on the matter. However, I shall be glad to go into the case again and consider it in the light of the representations which have been made here to-night. With regard to this item, my colleague the Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott) is anxious to introduce his estimates, and if the committee would care to pass it-
It is not necessary to pass it, you know.
-all right. If not that will be all right also.

Item agreed to.
POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT Civil Government-
Salaries, including the assistant deputy postmaster general and general superintendent of postal service at $7,500 a year from April 1, 1937; amounts required to pay allowances to office appliance operators, grade 2, operating mechanical audit card punching machines in accordance with the terms of order in council P.C. 280/383. dated February 17, 1930; to pay
Supply-Post Office

allowances to typists, grade 1, employed cutting stencils in accordance with regulations approved by order in council; and to pay allowances to office appliance operators, grade 2, in the revenue division employed as key punch operators, schedules and rates to be decided upon by the civil service commission and the post office department and approved by the governor in council, $1,318,488.
Contingencies, $215,000.
Hon, J. C. ELLIOTT (Postmaster General): Perhaps I should make a statement as to the increases. The item for salaries is $1,318,488, an increase of $69,828. The increase is accounted for by 391 statutory increases amounting to $27,540. If my hon. friends would like to have the details I can give them very readily, but they are the regular statutory increases. Then there is one special increase of $600 to augment the salary of the assistant deputy postmaster general and general superintendent of postal service to $7,500, effective April 1, 1937. There are fifty-two additional positions; these are required to provide an adequate establishment for the administrative services and financial branch. The positions were approved by the civil service commission and authorized by order in council dated July 10, 1936, and October 23, 1936. They will be filled by the civil service commission by promotional competition or appointment. What I have already given amounts to $27,540. There will be deducted three positions no longer required, amounting to S9,600, and the difference in salaries of employees who have left the service and the salaries of those who have replaced them, amounting to $1,620, and current salary deduction amounting to $2,952. There is a total of deductions of $14,000, making up the $69,828.

I notice this item in
the estimates of 1937-38 is No. 16, and in the estimates of 1936-37 it was No. 20. Looking through the auditor general's report of 193536, I find it scattered in three or four different places. It is almost impossible to check one item with the other so as to find out where we are going or what we have under discussion. An estimate appears for a large sum of money like this and about the only thing we can do is to ask the reason for the increase, or some question which has no more import than that. If we want to check over the figures contained in the previous year's item we have not yet the details. The latest report I have is the auditor general's report for 1935-36; next year we shall get the auditor general's report for last year, 1936-37, and the year following we shall get it for the item now under discussion. I do not know that anything can be done in the way of better bookkeeping 
than we have at present, but it is a nightmare to connect the items of this year with last year from the auditor general's report of 1935-36.

I want to ask the minister what led his department to decide that the postal employees of Canada should be compelled to work on statutory holidays. Undoubtedly a decision for which he is responsible was arrived at by his department, and he should make a statement.
That question can better be discussed under item 275 and I suggest that we defer the discussion until then.

In this connection I suggest that the minister bring down the return to the question asked him a few weeks ago and passed by the house. When may we expect that correspondence?

The great
volume of it is ready now, but it is not complete. I expect to be able to table the report within a short time.
A great volume is ready but the small volume is not.
A considerable volume still remains.

This covers superintendent of air and land mail services. Will the minister give us some information with regard to what air mail services there are now in Canada?

That also

What are the duties of the director of public relations of the Post Office Department?

Largely publicity, to endeavour to keep track of matters that are taking place in the various branches of the department and to give information concerning them from time to time. These duties are carried out with the fourfold object: increasing revenue; obtaining the cooperation of the mailing public; maintaining supervision over the various branches with the idea of creating an esprit de corps among the different branches, and the creating of good will.
Is the department carrying out an accounting system of its own showing complete revenue and complete disbursements as applied to the Post Office Department?

We have an accounting system that keeps track of the business in the department and that is under the supervision of the financial superintendent and for expenditure under the comptroller of the treasury.
Is the minister in a position to state, from his financial set-up showing revenues and disbursements, whether the Post Office Department pays it way?

I am in a
position to state that the department more than pays its way.
Except the dead letter department.
I may say that in the last year it more than paid its way. If time permitted, I should like to give my bon. friend the total revenues and expenditures for the past year. Perhaps I have time.
Time to start anyway.

The total estimated revenue for the year closing March 31, 1937, judging by the nine months that have passed, will be $41,178,199. From this we deduct $6,868,164 paid to commission postmasters, leaving net revenue $34,310,035. This represents an increase of $1,802,146 over the
preceding year. The outlay for the year is S30,100,101.63.
Does that include gross outlay or just the net?

No, that is outlay reckoned according to the system to which my hon. friend objects, but which has been in force since confederation. It does not include the item to which I know he refers, of rental for buildings-
Maintenance.
-maintenance of those buildings, including char service, coal and that sort of thing. Perhaps to clarify the matter-
The minister might break down the items at his convenience.

Yes. I should like to say a word in regard to that so as to give my hon. friend the information for which he asked.
